c.tagline: Algeria's Mediterranean second city, birthplace of raï music.

taxi.fareNote: Shared 'taxi collectif' cabs run set routes for a small fixed fare; for a private ride agree the price before setting off. The Yassir app is the easiest way to get a metered-style fare and avoid haggling.

emergency.note: 17 reaches the national police (Sûreté Nationale); 14 is the ambulance/emergency medical service. The gendarmerie can be reached on 1055.

avoid.reason: Avoid the harbor area and the unlit backstreets of the old Sidi El Houari quarter after dark.
Pickpocketing occurs in the Medina Jdida market crowds; keep valuables out of sight and avoid deserted streets at night.

hood_desc: The atmospheric old town on the slopes below Santa Cruz fort, Oran's Spanish- and Ottoman-era historic quarter with the Sidi El Houari mosque, faded colonial facades and steep lanes; rich in sights but rough around the edges.

The French-built city center around Place d'Armes (Place du 1er Novembre), the ornate Opera and Town Hall, tree-lined boulevards, cafes and the seafront promenade; the most convenient and walkable base for visitors.
A modern upscale seaside district to the west with newer hotels, apartment blocks, restaurants and a marina feel; a comfortable, quieter base near the water.
A cliff-top residential and leisure area near Santa Cruz and the Murdjadjo heights with sea views, cafes and the chapel; relaxed and scenic, better with a car.
The bustling popular market district built around the Médina Jedida bazaar, one of the country's biggest, packed with artisan goods and cheap eats; authentic, crowded and budget-friendly.
lodging: Le Méridien Oran Hotel & Convention Centre
Hôtel Four Points by Sheraton Oran

water.note: Stick to bottled water; tap quality and supply vary.

transit.hours: The tramway and city buses run from roughly 5:00 AM to around 11:00 PM; late-night travel relies on taxis and the Yassir app.
transit.note: Oran's modern tramway (opened 2013) links the university, city center and eastern suburbs, complemented by ETUSO city buses and abundant shared and private taxis. It is one of the few Algerian cities with a tram.
transit.pay: Buy tram tickets from station machines or kiosks; bus and taxi fares are paid in cash to the driver. Keep small dinar notes and coins handy.

landmarks: Fort Santa Cruz
A 16th-century Spanish fortress crowning Mount Murdjadjo, its ramparts deliver Oran's most sweeping panorama over the harbor, red rooftops and the shimmering Mediterranean.
Chapelle de Santa Cruz
Perched just below the fort, this 19th-century pilgrimage chapel with its towering Virgin statue was built in thanksgiving after a cholera epidemic spared the city.
Place du 1er Novembre (Place d'Armes)
Oran's elegant colonial heart, where a winged victory column stands between the ornate Hôtel de Ville, guarded by bronze lions, and the sumptuous opera house.
Théâtre Régional Abdelkader Alloula (Oran Opera House)
A lavish 1907 Belle Époque theater whose gilded ceilings, allegorical statues and plush red interiors evoke the grandeur of Paris on the Algerian coast.
Palais du Bey (Bey's Palace)
The 18th-century Ottoman residence of Bey Mohamed el-Kebir, an atmospheric complex of arcaded courtyards, painted ceilings and harem quarters overlooking the old lower town.
Cathédrale du Sacré-Cœur d'Oran
A striking Romano-Byzantine former cathedral completed in 1913, now a public library, whose domes and rose-tinted facade dominate a busy downtown square.
Mosquée du Pacha (Hassan Pasha Mosque)
Built in 1797 to celebrate the Spanish departure, this Ottoman mosque's octagonal minaret and serene tiled courtyard anchor the historic Sidi El Houari quarter.
Sidi El Houari Quarter
Oran's crumbling but soulful old town, a layered maze of Spanish gates, Ottoman houses and colonial facades named for the city's revered patron saint.
Musée National Ahmed Zabana
The city's premier museum pairs Roman mosaics and prehistoric finds with Orientalist paintings, natural history galleries and moving exhibits on Algeria's independence struggle.
Front de Mer (Boulevard de l'ALN)
A breezy clifftop promenade lined with grand colonial buildings, where Oranais stroll at sunset above the port with Santa Cruz glowing on the mountain.

train.note: There are no international trains from Algeria - the Moroccan border has been closed since 1994 and the Tunisian through service has not run for years. Domestically, SNTF's Coradia express trains link Oran with Algiers in about 4 hours and run south to Sidi Bel Abbès and Tlemcen. The station is central. Buy at the station or on the SNTF site.

intl.to: Tunis (Tunisia) - via Algiers and the Oum Teboul border
intl.op: SNTV / private Algerian operators — tickets at the Oran bus terminal, no online booking

bus.note: The only overland international route out of Algeria is east to Tunisia; the Moroccan border is closed. Domestic coaches from Oran's terminal reach Algiers in about 5 hours, Constantine and Tlemcen. Buy at the terminal in cash. A visa is required for Algeria for most nationalities and must be arranged before arrival.

ferry.note: Oran is one of Algeria's main passenger ports and the ferries to France are heavily used by the diaspora, especially in July and August when they book out months ahead. Crossings to Marseille take about a day and carry cars. The Alicante service is seasonal. Bring your passport and check Schengen visa requirements well in advance.

half.name: Mostaganem
half.blurb: A coastal town with Ottoman-era ramparts and cliffside beaches lies about an hour east of Oran.

half.name: Sidi Bel Abbès
half.blurb: A former French garrison town with wide colonial-era boulevards sits roughly an hour south of Oran.

half.name: Arzew
half.blurb: A port town with Spanish and Ottoman fortifications on the Gulf of Arzew lies about forty minutes away.

full.name: Tlemcen
full.blurb: A former Zayyanid capital with the Great Mosque and the Mansourah minaret ruins is about two and a half hours southwest.
